   agitation and felt that presentation was consistent with acute alcohol
   withdrawal. No more surgical issues per ortho therefore recommended
   transfer to medicine. On the floor, he received ativan 4mg total during

 see flowsheet. UOP increasing now >30ml/hr. 1600 dose of

 now 5mg PO Q1hr WA. Continue

   half empty bottle of Tequila. He is s/p an ORIF on [**9-18**]. After the

   CIWA (q2hrs). Psychiatry liason feels the symptoms are more c/w post-op
   delirium and recommend haldol and not using benzos in this elderly man.
   Medicine consulted for help in management of withdrawal symptoms and
   agitation and felt that presentation was consistent with acute alcohol
   withdrawal. No more surgical issues per ortho therefore recommended
   transfer to medicine. .
   On the floor, he received ativan 4mg total during the day, and then at
   time of severe agitation, he received 5mg over approximately one hour
   until sedated, which was brief. He was transferred to the MICU for
   further monitoring.
   Micu course involved significant valium treatment for S & S of acute
   alcohol withdrawal.
   Altered mental status (not Delirium)

s on the bed.  Does seem to

   groaning.

   awaiting results, bilateral wrist restraints  for security of lines

   this shift).

   Assessment:
   Pt with right shoulder rash and irritation/rash to bil arms.  Slightly

   assessment.

 INDICATION:  Osteomyelitis/endocarditis postop.  Evaluate for an abdominal
 source.

 No prior studies are available for comparison.

 TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous CT axial images are obtained from the lung bases
 through the pubic symphysis after the administration of 150 cc Optiray
 nonionic IV contrast.  Optiray was utilized given patient's history of high
 blood pressure.

 CT ABDOMEN WITH IV CONTRAST:  There are bilateral pleural effusions left
 greater than right.  There is atelectasis of the right lung adjacent to the
 effusion.  There is air and fluid behind the sternum.  This tracks inferiorly
 to the anterior aspect of the liver.  There are multiple, subcentimeter, low
 attenuation foci too small to characterize within the liver.  Two low
 attenuation foci are seen within the spleen, the one at the posterior tip
 causes a slight bulge in the splenic contour.  A calcification is seen in the
 pancreatic head.  There is no pancreatic duct dilatation or obstruction.  The
 adrenal glands and kidneys are grossly normal.  No free air or free fluid is
 seen within the abdomen.  No abnormal mesenteric or retroperitoneal
 lymphadenopathy is present.  The large and small bowel are well visualized and
 are grossly normal.

 CT PELVIS WITH IV CONTRAST:  The urinary bladder and ureters are unremarkable.
 The rectum and sigmoid colon are within normal limits.  There is no free air
 or free fluid within the pelvis.  Bone windows show mild degenerative changes
 throughout the thoracic spine and do not reflect the findings found on the MR
 of [**3-19**].

 IMPRESSION:
 1.  No intra-abdominal abscess or focus of infection.
 2.  Hypointense lesions within the liver are too small to accurately
 characterize on CT.  Differential includes cyst but abscess cannot be ruled
 out.  Investigation with ultrasound can delineate abscess from cyst, but many
 abscesses are not detected on ultrasound.
 3.  Hypodense lesions within the spleen are consistent with hemangioma, cyst,
 or abscess.  Because one lesion causes bulging of the splenic contour, it is
 unlikely to be an abscess.
